Bilirubin is a yellowish substance made during the normal breakdown of red blood cells; it passes through the liver and leaves the body in bile. A bilirubin test measures total bilirubin and sometimes direct (conjugated) and indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin. High levels can cause jaundice (yellow skin and eyes) and may be related to liver disease, blocked bile ducts or increased breakdown of red blood cells. Gilbert syndrome, a common inherited condition, can cause mildly raised bilirubin that is usually harmless.

A BUN test measures urea nitrogen, a waste product made when the liver breaks down protein and removed from the blood by the kidneys. It is often ordered with creatinine, for example in a basic metabolic panel, to check kidney function. A high BUN can occur with kidney disease, dehydration, a high-protein diet, heart failure, bleeding in the digestive tract or some medicines; a low BUN is less common and may be seen with liver disease or malnutrition. A BUN-to-creatinine ratio is sometimes reported to help interpretation.

A liver panel includes measurements of enzymes, proteins and bilirubin. ALT and AST are enzymes; albumin is a protein made by the liver. These results can provide information about liver injury or function, but a panel alone does not identify the cause of an abnormal result. Interpretation uses the pattern, other tests and clinical information.

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the best overall measure of kidney function, but it is rarely measured directly; instead it is estimated (eGFR) from serum creatinine using an equation that also uses age and sex. NIDDK recommends the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation, which does not include a race term. eGFR is reported in mL/min/1.73 m² and is less accurate when creatinine is not stable or in people with very high or very low muscle mass, where adding cystatin C can improve the estimate. eGFR is read together with urine albumin and over time.

A BUN test measures urea nitrogen, a waste product made when the liver breaks down protein and removed from the blood by the kidneys. It is often ordered with creatinine, for example in a basic metabolic panel, to check kidney function. A high BUN can occur with kidney disease, dehydration, a high-protein diet, heart failure, bleeding in the digestive tract or some medicines; a low BUN is less common and may be seen with liver disease or malnutrition. A BUN-to-creatinine ratio is sometimes reported to help interpretation.

NIDDK explains that early kidney disease usually has no symptoms, so blood and urine tests are the only way to know how the kidneys are working. A creatinine blood test is used to estimate the glomerular filtration rate (eGFR): an eGFR of 60 or more is in the normal range, below 60 may mean kidney disease, and 15 or less may mean kidney failure. A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) below 30 mg/g is normal, while 30 mg/g or more may be a sign of kidney disease. Because results can change for temporary reasons, abnormal tests are repeated over about 3 months to confirm kidney disease.

KDIGO classifies CKD by cause, GFR category and albuminuria category. GFR categories in mL/min/1.73 m² are G1 90 or above, G2 60 to 89, G3a 45 to 59, G3b 30 to 44, G4 15 to 29 and G5 below 15 (kidney failure). Albuminuria categories by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio are A1 below 30 mg/g, A2 30 to 300 mg/g and A3 above 300 mg/g. G1 and G2 count as CKD only when markers of kidney damage are present, and a category is assigned only after abnormalities have lasted more than 3 months.

KDIGO defines chronic kidney disease (CKD) as abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for more than 3 months with implications for health. A GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², or one or more markers of kidney damage such as albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 30 mg/g or 3 mg/mmol or more), abnormal urine sediment, abnormalities on imaging or a history of kidney transplantation, meets the definition when it lasts longer than 3 months. A single abnormal result is therefore not a diagnosis; tests are repeated to show that the change persists.

Chloride is an electrolyte that works with sodium, potassium and bicarbonate to help control the body's fluid balance and acid-base balance. It is usually measured in an electrolyte panel or metabolic panel, and its level often changes in the same direction as sodium. Abnormal chloride levels can be linked to dehydration, prolonged vomiting or diarrhea, kidney problems, acid-base disturbances or some medicines. Chloride is interpreted with the other electrolytes rather than on its own.

A lipid panel measures cholesterol and triglycerides. LDL and HDL carry cholesterol in the blood. Interpretation considers cardiovascular risk factors and the full profile, not a single value alone. Fasting requirements depend on the ordered test and laboratory instructions. A calculated result and a directly measured result should not be treated as interchangeable.

NHLBI explains that high blood cholesterol usually has no signs or symptoms, so a blood test called a lipid panel is used to measure total cholesterol, LDL ("bad") cholesterol, HDL ("good") cholesterol and triglycerides. Some lipid tests require fasting beforehand, depending on the instructions given. A clinician looks at the results together with other risk factors for heart disease and stroke, such as age, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and family history, rather than at one number alone.

The American Heart Association explains that cholesterol is a waxy substance the body needs to build cells and is carried in the blood by lipoproteins: LDL, which can contribute to plaque build-up in the arteries, and HDL, which helps remove excess cholesterol. Triglycerides are another type of fat in the blood. The AHA advises adults aged 20 and older to have cholesterol and other traditional risk factors checked every 4 to 6 years if their risk remains low, and cholesterol numbers are considered together with other risk factors to estimate the risk of heart attack and stroke.

HDL (high-density lipoprotein) is called "good" cholesterol because it carries cholesterol from other parts of the body back to the liver, which removes it from the body. Higher HDL levels are generally linked to a lower risk of heart disease, and a low HDL is one of the risk factors a clinician considers. MedlinePlus lists a healthy HDL level for adults as 40 mg/dL or higher for men and 50 mg/dL or higher for women. HDL is measured in a lipid panel and read together with LDL, triglycerides and other risk factors.

A creatinine blood test is used to estimate the glomerular filtration rate (eGFR): an eGFR of 60 or more is in the normal range, below 60 may mean kidney disease, and 15 or less may mean kidney failure. A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) below 30 mg/g is normal, while 30 mg/g or more may be a sign of kidney disease. Because results can change for temporary reasons, abnormal tests are repeated over about 3 months to confirm kidney disease.

A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio compares urine albumin with urine creatinine to help identify kidney damage. Transient factors can affect albumin in urine, so an abnormal result may require repeat testing and clinical assessment. Preserve the reported unit and ratio; a urine concentration alone is not the same as the ratio.

KDIGO defines chronic kidney disease (CKD) as abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for more than 3 months with implications for health. A GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², or one or more markers of kidney damage such as albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 30 mg/g or 3 mg/mmol or more), abnormal urine sediment, abnormalities on imaging or a history of kidney transplantation, meets the definition when it lasts longer than 3 months. A single abnormal result is therefore not a diagnosis; tests are repeated to show that the change persists.

KDIGO classifies CKD by cause, GFR category and albuminuria category. GFR categories in mL/min/1.73 m² are G1 90 or above, G2 60 to 89, G3a 45 to 59, G3b 30 to 44, G4 15 to 29 and G5 below 15 (kidney failure). Albuminuria categories by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio are A1 below 30 mg/g, A2 30 to 300 mg/g and A3 above 300 mg/g. G1 and G2 count as CKD only when markers of kidney damage are present, and a category is assigned only after abnormalities have lasted more than 3 months.

Creatinine is a waste product associated with muscle activity that kidneys remove from blood. Blood or urine creatinine measurements help assess kidney function. Muscle mass, diet and other factors can influence the result. A clinician may combine creatinine with other information, including an estimated filtration rate, rather than interpreting a single value alone.

A complete blood count measures blood cells and related indices. Hemoglobin carries oxygen; hematocrit describes the red-cell share of blood volume; MCV describes average red-cell size. White-cell and platelet counts provide different information. Results can be affected by hydration, medicines and other factors, so a pattern requires clinical context and sometimes additional tests.

A white blood count measures the number of white blood cells, which help the body fight infections and other diseases, and is part of a complete blood count. A differential count shows the main types: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. A high count can occur with infection, inflammation, stress, some medicines or, less commonly, blood disorders; a low count can occur with some viral infections, autoimmune conditions, bone-marrow problems or certain medical treatments. A single result is interpreted with symptoms and other tests.

Platelets (thrombocytes) are small blood cells that help blood clot to stop bleeding, and a platelet count is usually part of a complete blood count. A low count (thrombocytopenia) can increase the risk of bruising or bleeding and may be linked to certain infections, medicines, autoimmune conditions, bone-marrow problems or an enlarged spleen. A high count (thrombocytosis) can occur with inflammation, infection, iron deficiency or bone-marrow disorders. Further tests may be needed to find the cause of an abnormal count.

Thrombocytopenia is a condition in which the platelet count in the blood is lower than normal. Platelets help blood clot, so a low count can cause easy bruising, tiny red-purple spots on the skin (petechiae) or prolonged bleeding, although a mild decrease may cause no symptoms. It can result from the bone marrow making too few platelets, from the body destroying platelets (for example in some autoimmune conditions or with some medicines or infections) or from platelets being trapped in an enlarged spleen. A complete blood count finds the low count, and other tests look for the cause.
